title: How do you prepare staff training and qualification evidence for NQF assessment and rating?
description: How authorized officers observe, sight, and discuss practice in NQF assessment and rating visits, the staff records they check, and a preparation checklist.
shortAnswer: To prepare for assessment and rating under Australia's National Quality Framework (NQF), keep staff records showing approved qualifications, early childhood teacher coverage, current first aid, anaphylaxis and asthma training, child safety training, and Working with Children Checks, and keep your self-assessment or quality improvement plan current. State and territory regulatory authorities conduct the visits against the National Quality Standard on short notice, and authorized officers observe practice, sight documents, and discuss practice with educators.
keyTakeaways: Assessment and rating is carried out by the state or territory regulatory authority against the National Quality Standard; the Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority (ACECQA) is the national authority that sets qualification requirements and guidance.
In New South Wales the notice period for assessment and rating visits has been 5 business days since July 2024, and partial reassessments usually cover 4 of the 7 quality areas.

Authorized officers rate services on what they observe, sight, and discuss; NSW lists staffing records, including Working with Children Checks and qualifications, among documents officers may ask to sight.
First aid, anaphylaxis, and emergency asthma training are current for three years, and CPR for one year, since 1 October 2023.
National child safety training became mandatory from 27 February 2026, with a refresher every two years, and authorized officers may check certificates.

sections.heading: Who conducts assessment and rating, and against what?

blocks.text: Assessment and rating is conducted by the regulatory authority in each state and territory, using authorized officers who rate a service against each quality area of the National Quality Standard. In New South Wales the regulator is the NSW Early Learning Commission, which says on its [assessment and rating page](https://education.nsw.gov.au/early-childhood-education/regulation-and-compliance/assessment-and-rating) that it collaborates with other jurisdictions and with ACECQA, the national authority, for a coherent approach under the National Law and Regulations. NSW is used as the worked example on this page; other regulators publish their own procedures.

The NSW page explains that authorized officers give a quality rating in each quality area and an overall rating "based on what they observe, cite, and discuss with services during a scheduled visit," and that officers confirm the key practice points in the service's self-assessment or quality improvement plan by having conversations, observing practice, and sighting documentation.

sections.heading: How does an assessment and rating visit work?

blocks.text: In NSW, a service is notified 5 business days before the visit, told whether it is a full assessment or a partial reassessment, and then visited by an authorized officer who tours the service, observes, sights documents, and talks with educators. The steps below come from the NSW regulator's published pages and its [factsheet for centre-based educators](https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/early-childhood-education/operating-an-early-childhood-education-service/media/documents/regulation-assessment-rating/assessment_and_rating_centre_based_educators_factsheet.pdf).

items: **Self-assessment or quality improvement plan (QIP).** The Commission may request a service's self-assessment information or QIP at any time, and the most recently submitted version supports officers' visits.

**Notice.** Since July 2024 the notice period is 5 business days. Partial reassessments usually cover 4 of the 7 quality areas, and services may nominate one quality area when asked for their self-assessment or QIP, except where assessment follows a serious incident.

**Visit.** The officer shows ID, signs the visitor record, explains the visit, asks for a tour of all areas used for education and care, observes interactions, asks to see documents, and talks with educators.
**Draft report.** The officer prepares a draft report with provisional ratings, which is peer reviewed and approved before it goes to the approved provider.

**Feedback.** The approved provider has 10 working days from the date the draft report is issued to submit feedback on factual inaccuracies or critical omissions, with supporting evidence, before the final report and ratings are issued.

blocks.text: NSW has also announced that its inactive assessment and rating periods (set periods without routine visits) will be removed from January 2027.

sections.heading: What do officers ask about staff training and qualifications?

blocks.text: Officers sight staffing records and talk with educators about their knowledge, so training evidence needs to be both on file and in people's heads. The NSW factsheet lists staffing records, "including Working with Children Checks (WWCC) and qualifications," and documents required under regulation 177 of the Education and Care Services National Regulations among the documents an officer may want to sight.

The same factsheet says officers may talk to educators about staffing arrangements, "child safe practices, including your understanding of child protection requirements," and their knowledge and understanding of the service's policies and procedures. Officers also observe how staff implement policies and procedures and check first aid kits.

blocks.text: The qualification rules are explained in full on the [NQF educator qualifications page](/regulations/national-quality-framework-educator-qualifications), and child protection and child safety training on the [NSW child protection training page](/regulations/child-protection-training-early-childhood-nsw).

sections.heading: What should a service check before notice arrives?

blocks.text: Five business days is not enough time to chase expired certificates, so treat readiness as continuous. This original checklist combines the documents NSW officers may sight with the qualification and training rules above.

items: Reconcile the staff record against the current roster: every educator has a qualification or documented actively working towards status, and every WWCC number is recorded and current.
Check first aid, anaphylaxis, asthma, and CPR expiry dates for everyone counted toward the regulation 136 requirement, and set reminders 60 days before expiry.
Confirm national child safety training completion for every person who needs it, with certificates filed, and plan refreshers on the two year cycle.
Update the self-assessment and QIP so they describe what actually happens, since officers use them to frame questions.

Brief educators on the policies they will be asked about, especially child protection, mandatory reporting, and medical conditions. A [training matrix for a childcare service](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-a-childcare-service) helps track who needs what.
Keep regulation 177 documents and staffing records easy to reach in paper or electronic form, as the NSW factsheet recommends.
Prepare to give feedback on the draft report within 10 working days, with evidence limited to factual inaccuracies or critical omissions.

blocks.text: After the visit the approved provider receives a draft report with provisional ratings, can submit feedback within 10 working days, and then receives the final report and ratings. NSW also sends every service a post visit survey, with 10 business days to respond; responses are not shared with the authorized officer and do not affect ratings. NSW has introduced limits on how much supporting evidence can accompany feedback, so feedback should be specific and relevant.

If staff training gaps were noted, update the QIP with dated actions and keep the evidence of completion, since the next request for the QIP can come at any time. For the wider method of auditing your own records first, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry turns service policies and regulatory requirements into role based learning outcomes and checks, so a provider can show which educators understand child protection, medical conditions, and other policies, not only who holds a certificate. See [operational procedures programs](/programs/operational-procedures) and [compliance programs](/programs/compliance).

faqs.a: Assessment and rating visits are conducted by authorized officers of the state or territory regulatory authority. ACECQA is the national authority that works with those regulators, approves qualifications and training, and publishes national guidance such as the Guide to the National Quality Framework.

faqs.q: How much notice does a service get?
faqs.a: In NSW, 5 business days since July 2024, and the service is told within that notice period whether the visit is a full assessment or a partial reassessment. Postponement is considered only in exceptional circumstances under the regulator's scheduling policy. Other jurisdictions set their own practice.

Yes. NSW guidance says officers talk with staff, observe practice on the day, and sight documents. Topics can include routines and the educational program, staffing arrangements, child safe practices and child protection requirements, and educators' understanding of the service's policies and procedures.

faqs.q: Does in-house first aid training count?
faqs.a: Only approved training satisfies regulation 136. ACECQA approves first aid, anaphylaxis management, and emergency asthma management training, and non-approved training does not meet the requirement. Keep certificates that show the approved course and completion date.

Post visit: survey with 10 business days, not shared with officer and no bearing on ratings; draft report with provisional ratings peer reviewed and approved; approved provider has 10 working days to submit feedback on factual inaccuracies or critical omissions; limits on supporting evidence.

Factsheet: officer shows ID, signs visitor record, explains visit, tours, observes, sights documents, talks with staff; documents include regulation 177 documents and staffing records including WWCC and qualifications; topics include staffing arrangements, child safe practices including child protection understanding, policies and procedures; first aid kits checked; documents easily accessible recommended.
